title: Soap Making (Laundry & Bath Soap): Production for Small Business

modules.title: Soap Chemistry, Materials and Safety for Production
modules.overview: Before you scale up, you need to know why a laundry bar and a bath bar are built differently, how to judge your raw materials, how to keep a production space safe with several kilograms of caustic soda, and how to turn any formula into exact grams. This module gives you that foundation.

lessons.title: How soap cleans, and why laundry bars and bath bars are built differently
objectives: Explain saponification and how a soap molecule lifts oily dirt
Name the fatty acids that make a bar hard, cleansing or conditioning
Compare the design goals of a laundry bar and a bath bar
Predict how hard water affects soap and what to do about it

blocks.text: Every true soap is made by reacting **fats or oils** with a strong alkali. For bars, the alkali is **sodium hydroxide**, sold in Nigerian markets as caustic soda. The reaction is called **saponification**. It turns oil and caustic soda into two things: **soap** and **glycerin**. When the amounts are right, no free caustic soda is left in the finished bar.

blocks.name: bar-of-soap
blocks.caption: The same reaction makes a hard laundry bar and a gentle bath bar; the choice of oils and superfat makes the difference.

blocks.text: How a soap molecule cleans

A soap molecule has two ends. One end loves water. The other end loves oil and grease. When you rub soap into a stained cloth, the oil-loving ends grab the grease, and the water-loving ends face outward. Many molecules gather round each droplet of grease to form a tiny ball called a **micelle**. Rinsing water then carries these balls away, with the dirt trapped inside.
Sodium soaps, made with caustic soda, are firm. Potassium soaps, made with caustic potash, are soft or liquid. That is why everything in this course uses caustic soda: we are making bars.
The fatty acids that decide how a bar behaves
Each oil is a mix of fatty acids, and each fatty acid gives the soap a different personality. You do not need to memorise chemistry; you need to know which oils bring which quality.

head: Fatty acids
Main local sources
What they give the bar
rows: Hard bar, quick big lather, strong cleansing (can dry skin)
Hard, long-lasting bar with creamy, stable lather
Olive oil, groundnut oil, palm oil (part)
Boosts lather; used in small amounts
Silky feel but can go rancid and cause orange spots

blocks.text: Two products, two design goals

A **laundry bar** works on fabric, not skin. You want it to cut grease and sweat strongly, stay hard in a wet bucket, and not leave oil on clothes. So laundry bars use a high share of PKO or coconut oil and very little spare oil. A **bath bar** touches skin every day. You want it to clean gently and leave skin comfortable, so it balances cleansing oils with conditioning oils and keeps more spare, unreacted oil in the bar.

That spare oil is called the **superfat**. A superfat of 5% means you use 5% less caustic soda than the oils could take, so about 5% of the oil stays as oil. Soap Queen, a long-running soap makers' resource, recommends about 5% for ordinary bath bars and no more than 3% for laundry soap, because extra oil can stain clothes and go rancid.

blocks.title: Laundry bar versus bath bar
items: Laundry bar
Bath bar
blocks.caption: The method is the same; the oil blend and superfat are chosen for fabric or for skin.

blocks.text: Soap and hard water

In hard water, which carries dissolved calcium and magnesium, part of the soap reacts with these minerals to form **soap scum**, the grey film you see on buckets. The scum wastes soap and can leave clothes dull. Borehole water in many parts of Nigeria can be hard. Two practical answers: use rain water or softer water for washing where possible, or add **washing soda** (sodium carbonate) to the wash water, which you will use in Module 2 to make laundry powder.

blocks.title: Worked example: deciding what each product needs
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi in Onitsha already sells palm oil. Customers ask her for a cheap bar for washing clothes and a nice bar for the bath. She plans one formula for each.
steps: For the laundry bar she writes: main oil PKO for cleansing, some palm oil for hardness and slower wear, superfat 2% so clothes are not left oily.
For the bath bar she writes: palm oil for a hard creamy bar, PKO limited to about a fifth of the oils so it is not drying, olive and shea for conditioning, castor oil for lather, superfat 5%.
She notes that the laundry bar needs no fragrance, which saves money, while the bath bar will carry a light scent.
She tests the water in her shop's borehole by washing a white cloth with a sample bar. A grey film forms in the bowl, so she plans to sell washing soda powder beside the bars.
blocks.result: Ngozi has two clear design briefs before she buys a single kilogram of oil, which stops her from making one bar that does neither job well.

blocks.title: Not every cleaning product is soap
blocks.text: Most liquid detergents, dish washes and many washing powders sold in Nigeria are **synthetic detergents** made from chemicals such as sulphonic acid, not oils and caustic soda. They behave differently in hard water. This course is about true soap made from oils.

takeaways: Soap = oils + caustic soda, giving soap and glycerin
PKO and coconut oil give cleansing and hardness; palm and shea give hardness and creamy lather; olive gives mildness
Laundry bars: high cleansing, superfat 3% or less
Bath bars: balanced oils, superfat about 5%
Hard water forms scum; washing soda helps

activity.title: Write two design briefs
steps: Ask three customers or neighbours what they want from a laundry bar and from a bath bar.
Write one short brief for each: purpose, main oils, superfat, scent.
Check each brief against the table of fatty acids in this lesson.
Test your local washing water: wash a white cloth with any soap and look for grey scum.
activity.evidence: A photo of your two written briefs and a note on whether your water formed scum

lessons.title: Buying and checking oils, caustic soda and water for production
objectives: Choose oils for laundry and bath bars and check their quality before buying
Read a caustic soda label and correct for purity
Pick suitable water and store materials so they stay usable
Keep a simple supplier and materials record

blocks.text: At home you might buy one bottle of oil at a time. In production you buy in kegs, drums and bags, so a bad purchase hurts more. This lesson shows what to check for each raw material and how to store it.

blocks.name: gone-shopping
blocks.caption: Buy raw materials with a checklist in hand, not on trust alone.

blocks.text: Oils

items: **Palm kernel oil (PKO):** the backbone of Nigerian laundry bars. It should be clear to light yellow when warm and smell clean and nutty. A sharp or sour smell means it is going rancid.
**Palm oil:** gives hardness and slow wear. Red palm oil colours soap orange; this is fine for laundry bars. Bleached palm oil gives a paler bar for bath soap.
**Coconut oil:** similar cleansing to PKO, usually costs more in most Nigerian markets; use whichever is better value near you.
**Shea butter:** a conditioning, hardening butter for bath bars. Unrefined shea should smell nutty and smoky, not sour.
**Olive and castor oil:** used in smaller amounts in bath bars. Check the bottle is sealed and in date.

blocks.text: Never use oil that has been used for frying. Food particles and breakdown products make soap smell bad and spoil faster. Avoid oils sold in unlabelled, reused containers that once held chemicals.
Caustic soda

Caustic soda is sold as **flakes, pearls or solid lumps** in sealed bags or tubs. Buy from a chemical seller who keeps it sealed and dry. It absorbs water and carbon dioxide from the air, especially in humid weather, and slowly loses strength. Signs of a bad bag: wet, sticky or clumped flakes, or a crusty white coating.

Many bags print the **purity** (assay), for example 98% or 99%. Soap calculators assume 100% pure sodium hydroxide. If your bag says 98%, divide the calculated amount by 0.98 to get the flakes you actually weigh. If there is no purity on the bag, you cannot be sure of the strength, so test a small batch first and check the bars carefully.

blocks.title: Worked example: correcting for caustic soda purity
blocks.context: For example, Amina in Kano calculates that her laundry run needs 1,625 g of pure sodium hydroxide. Her 25 kg bag is labelled 98% purity.
steps: She divides the pure amount by the purity: 1,625 / 0.98 = 1,658 g (rounded).
She weighs 1,658 g of flakes, not 1,625 g.
She writes on her batch sheet: purity 98%, corrected caustic soda 1,658 g.
Next month she buys a different brand labelled 99% and recalculates: 1,625 / 0.99 = 1,641 g.
blocks.result: Amina's bars receive the sodium hydroxide the recipe intends, even when the brand changes. A 33 g difference on one run is enough to change how mild or oily a bar feels.

blocks.text: Water

Use **clean, soft water**: distilled water, rain water collected in a clean container and filtered, or boiled and cooled tap or borehole water. Hard or iron-rich water can cause spots and scum in the bar. Sachet or bottled water is acceptable for small test batches.
Storage and records

blocks.title: From supplier to batch
items: Check and buy
Label with date
Store cool and sealed
Use oldest first
Record on batch sheet
blocks.caption: Every material moves through the same simple path so you can trace any problem back to its source.

items: Store oils in closed containers, out of sun, and use the oldest stock first (first in, first out).
Store caustic soda sealed, raised off the floor, away from water, acids and aluminium, and out of reach of children.
Write the supplier, date bought, price and any purity or batch number on each container.
Keep a one-page materials log. When a batch goes wrong, the log tells you which keg or bag to suspect.

head: Material
Check before buying
Red flag
rows: Sour smell, water layer at the bottom
Sour or musty smell, visible dirt
Wet or clumped flakes, open bag

blocks.text: Flakes, pearls and liquid caustic soda

Flakes and pearls weigh and dissolve in much the same way, so choose whichever your supplier keeps fresh and sealed. Large solid lumps are hard to weigh accurately and dangerous to break, so avoid them. Some sellers offer caustic soda already dissolved in water in kegs. Its strength is usually unknown, so you cannot calculate a formula from it. For bar soap, buy dry, labelled flakes or pearls.
Buy oils in amounts you can use within a few months and store well. A drum that sits half-used for a year in a hot store may go rancid, and that waste cancels any bulk discount.

blocks.title: Do not decant caustic soda into food or drink containers
blocks.text: Keep caustic soda in its original bag or a strong, clearly labelled plastic tub with a tight lid. People in Nigeria have been seriously injured by swallowing caustic soda kept in drink bottles. Mark every container "CAUSTIC SODA, POISON, KEEP AWAY FROM CHILDREN".

takeaways: Fresh, clean oils make bars that last; never use frying oil
Correct caustic soda for purity: divide by 0.98 for 98%
Damp, clumped caustic soda has lost strength
Use soft, clean water
Log supplier, date and purity for every material

activity.title: Start your materials log
steps: Visit or call two suppliers of PKO and caustic soda and note their prices and pack sizes.
Look at a caustic soda bag and find the purity figure, or note that it is missing.
Smell and look at an oil sample using the table in this lesson.
Create a one-page materials log with columns: material, supplier, date, price, purity or batch, notes.
activity.evidence: A photo of your materials log with at least two supplier entries

lessons.title: Running a safe soap workspace when you scale up
objectives: Set up a production area with safe zones for lye, heat and drying
Wear and maintain the right protective equipment
Give correct first aid for caustic soda splashes and swallowing
Handle hot soap and gas burners safely during hot process

blocks.text: A small business may mix more than 1.5 kg of caustic soda in one go. The solution gets very hot and gives off fumes. In hot process you also cook soap paste over a flame for an hour or more. The risks are the same as at home, but larger. This lesson turns safety into a fixed routine.

blocks.name: goggles
blocks.caption: Sealed goggles stay on from the moment the caustic soda bag opens until the soap is in the mould.

blocks.text: Protective equipment

items: **Sealed chemical splash goggles**, not ordinary glasses. A face shield on top is wise when mixing large lye solutions.
**Long nitrile or rubber gloves** covering the wrists. Replace them when torn.
**Long sleeves, apron, trousers or long wrapper, closed shoes.** Synthetic fabrics melt near flames; cotton is safer around the burner.
**Dust mask** while weighing flakes or pouring washing soda powder.

blocks.text: Laying out the space

blocks.title: Safe production layout
items: Locked chemical store
Weighing table
Ventilated lye station
Oil and cooking area
Moulds and drying racks
blocks.caption: Materials move in one direction so caustic soda never crosses paths with food, children or customers.

items: Mix lye outdoors or under a roof with open sides, upwind of yourself. Never in a closed kitchen.
Keep a clear path between lye station and cooking area so you are not carrying hot solution past people.
Put the gas cylinder outside the room or at least 1 metre from the burner, and check hoses for cracks.
Keep children, pets and visitors out of the area during production. Put a sign on the door.
Keep a fire extinguisher or a bucket of sand near the burner. Never pour water on burning oil.

blocks.text: Mixing lye at production scale

items: Put on goggles, gloves and sleeves before opening the bag.
Weigh the water into a strong stainless steel or heavy HDPE plastic container (recycling numbers 2 or 5). Use cold water; in hot weather some makers use part ice.
Weigh the caustic soda in a separate dry container.
**Add the caustic soda to the water, slowly, stirring with a stainless spoon. Never pour water onto caustic soda.**
Step back from the fumes for a minute. The solution can heat above 80 degrees Celsius.
Cover loosely, label it, and let it cool where it cannot be knocked over.

blocks.text: Never use aluminium, tin or zinc pots or spoons. The US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) lists these metals as reacting dangerously with sodium hydroxide; aluminium releases flammable hydrogen gas.

blocks.title: First aid for caustic soda
blocks.text: **Skin:** remove soaked clothing and flush with plenty of running water straight away, for at least 15 minutes. Do not use vinegar; water is the correct treatment. **Eyes:** rinse immediately with clean running water for at least 15 minutes, holding the eyelids open, then go to hospital. **Swallowed:** rinse the mouth, do not make the person vomit, and get medical help immediately. **Fumes:** move to fresh air. Keep a large container of clean water or a running tap within reach every time you work.
Hot process adds heat risks

items: Use a heavy-bottomed stainless steel pot no more than about two-thirds full. Soap paste can swell and foam over.
Keep the flame low. Stir with a long stainless paddle so your arms stay away from the pot.
Hot soap paste sticks to skin and burns like hot porridge. Treat burns with cool running water for 20 minutes and seek care for large burns.
Never leave a pot on the flame unattended.

blocks.text: Cleaning up after a run

items: Keep goggles and gloves on while cleaning. Soap paste on pots and paddles is still caustic until it has fully reacted.
Scrape leftover paste into a mould or tray rather than washing it down the drain, and let it harden.
Wash tools in hot water with gloves on; many makers let used tools sit for a day so leftover paste turns into soap and washes off easily.
Rinse empty caustic soda bags or tubs, close them and keep them away from children before disposal. Never reuse them for food or water.
Wipe tables and floors with a damp cloth to pick up stray flakes, which can burn bare feet.

blocks.title: Worked example: a near miss and the rule that followed
blocks.context: For example, Funmi and her two helpers in Ibadan run a weekly laundry soap batch in a rented shop.
steps: A helper carried a 5 litre jug of fresh lye solution past the burner. Her glove caught the pot handle and a few drops splashed onto her forearm.
Funmi took her straight to the tap and rinsed the arm for 15 minutes by the clock while the other helper turned off the gas.
The skin was red but not broken; they watched it for the rest of the day.
Funmi changed the layout: the lye now cools on a low table outside, and is only carried in a lidded container with two hands, after everyone is warned.
She added a rule to the wall chart: long sleeves for everyone, not only the person mixing.
blocks.result: A small splash was treated correctly and led to a permanent change in layout. Funmi records near misses in her batch book so every helper learns from them.

takeaways: Goggles, long gloves, sleeves and closed shoes every time
Caustic soda into water, never water into caustic soda
No aluminium, tin or zinc
First aid is running water for at least 15 minutes; eyes go to hospital
Hot process needs a low flame, a deep pot and constant attention

activity.title: Draw and check your safety layout
steps: Sketch your space showing chemical store, weighing table, lye station, burner and drying racks.
Mark where the water tap or water drum, fire extinguisher or sand, and first aid card will be.
List the protective equipment you own and what you still need to buy.
Write the first aid steps on a card and put it on the wall.
activity.evidence: A photo of your layout sketch and the first aid card on the wall

lessons.title: Calculating formulas: SAP values, superfat, water and scaling up
objectives: Write a formula as percentages and convert it to grams for any batch size
Calculate caustic soda from SAP values and apply a superfat
Calculate water from a chosen lye concentration
Check your figures with the SoapCalc calculator

blocks.text: Professional soap makers write formulas as **percentages of the total oil weight**, not as cups or tins. Percentages let you make a 1 kg test batch today and a 10 kg production run next week from the same formula, with no guessing.

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.alt: A person working with a large calculator
blocks.caption: Every batch starts on paper or in a calculator, never by eye.

blocks.text: The four numbers in every formula

items: **Oil percentages:** for example 70% PKO and 30% palm oil. They must add up to 100%.
**SAP value** for each oil: grams of sodium hydroxide that 1 g of that oil needs to become soap.
**Superfat:** the percentage you reduce the caustic soda by, so some oil stays free.
**Lye concentration:** caustic soda as a percentage of the caustic soda plus water. 33% is a common, workable figure.

head: Oil
Sodium hydroxide SAP (g per g oil)

blocks.text: These are typical values that match published saponification ranges. Real oils vary a little from batch to batch, which is one reason a small superfat is used even in laundry bars. Always confirm your final recipe in the free **SoapCalc** calculator (soapcalc.net) before you make it.

blocks.title: From formula to batch sheet
items: Percentages to grams
Grams times SAP
Subtract superfat
Divide by purity
Calculate water
blocks.caption: Follow the same five steps every time, in this order.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 1 kg laundry test batch at two superfats
blocks.context: For example, Blessing in Aba wants to test a laundry formula of 70% PKO and 30% palm oil before making a big run. She makes a 1,000 g test batch.
steps: Grams of oil: PKO 70% of 1,000 g = 700 g; palm oil 30% = 300 g.
Caustic soda at 0% superfat: 700 x 0.176 = 123.2 g; 300 x 0.142 = 42.6 g; total 165.8 g.
At 2% superfat (laundry): 165.8 x 0.98 = 162.5 g.
For comparison, at 5% superfat (bath): 165.8 x 0.95 = 157.5 g. The difference is only 5 g per kilogram of oil.
Water at 33% lye concentration: 162.5 x 67 / 33 = 330 g (rounded).
Her caustic soda is 98% pure, so she weighs 162.5 / 0.98 = 165.8 g, rounded to 166 g of flakes.
blocks.result: Blessing's test batch sheet reads: PKO 700 g, palm oil 300 g, caustic soda flakes 166 g (98%), water 330 g, superfat 2%. Because 5 g changes the superfat by 3 points, she uses a scale that reads in 1 g steps.

blocks.text: Why the water formula works

Lye concentration is caustic soda divided by (caustic soda + water). If the caustic soda is 33 parts, the water must be 67 parts. So water = caustic soda x 67 / 33. Less water (higher concentration) gives a harder bar sooner but traces faster. More water gives more working time. For hot process, many makers use a little extra water so the paste stays workable during the cook.
Weighing and rounding rules

items: Weigh every ingredient, including water, in grams. Never measure caustic soda or oils by cups, tins or spoons.
Round caustic soda to the nearest whole gram only at the final step. Keep one decimal place in the working.
Tare (zero) the scale with the empty container on it before each weighing.
Write each weight on the batch sheet as you weigh it, and tick it. If you are interrupted, you will know where you stopped.
For a production run, ask a second person to read back the caustic soda weight before it goes into the water.

blocks.text: Choose the superfat by product. In this course we use **2% for laundry bars** (within the 3% maximum recommended for laundry soap) and **5% for bath bars**. A very small superfat in a laundry bar is a safety margin: oils vary slightly and scales are not perfect, so a 0% formula can end up with a little free caustic soda.
Scaling up

To scale, multiply every gram figure by the same factor, or go back to percentages. A 10 kg run of Blessing's formula is simply ten times the 1 kg sheet: 7,000 g PKO, 3,000 g palm oil, and the caustic soda and water recalculated in the same way. Recalculate rather than multiply rounded numbers, so small rounding errors do not grow.

blocks.title: Never swap the alkali
blocks.text: SAP values for sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are different. A recipe calculated for one must never be made with the other. If an online recipe does not say which it uses, do not use it.

blocks.title: Check in SoapCalc
blocks.text: In SoapCalc, choose NaOH, enter your oil weights, set the superfat and lye concentration, and press Calculate. Compare its caustic soda figure with yours. A difference of 1 or 2 g per kilogram comes from slightly different SAP values; a large difference means a mistake.

takeaways: Write formulas as percentages of oil weight
Caustic soda = sum of (oil x SAP), then x (1 minus superfat)
Water = caustic soda x 67 / 33 at 33% concentration
Divide by purity to get flakes to weigh
Confirm in SoapCalc before every new formula

activity.title: Build your first batch sheet
steps: Choose a laundry formula using two oils from the SAP table.
Calculate caustic soda at 0% and at 2% superfat for 1,000 g of oils.
Calculate water at 33% lye concentration and correct for your caustic soda purity.
Enter the same recipe in SoapCalc and note any difference.

quiz.q: Grace wants a laundry bar that will not leave oil marks on white shirts. Which superfat fits best?
quiz.explain: Laundry soap should have a low superfat, no more than about 3%. Higher spare oil can stain fabric and go rancid.

quiz.q: Which oil brings strong cleansing and a quick lather because it is rich in lauric acid?
quiz.explain: PKO, like coconut oil, is rich in lauric and myristic acids, which give hardness and strong cleansing.

quiz.q: A recipe needs 1,000 g of pure sodium hydroxide. The bag says 98% purity. How much should she weigh?
quiz.explain: Divide the pure amount by the purity: 1,000 / 0.98 = 1,020 g (rounded).

quiz.q: Caustic soda splashes into a helper's eye. What is the right first action?
options: Rinse with vinegar to neutralise it
Rinse with clean running water for at least 15 minutes, then go to hospital
Wipe it with a dry cloth and wait
Put eye drops in and continue working
quiz.explain: Eyes must be flushed immediately with plenty of running water for at least 15 minutes, holding the lids open, then seen at a hospital. Never use vinegar.

quiz.q: A test batch has 600 g PKO (SAP 0.176) and 400 g palm oil (SAP 0.142). What is the caustic soda at 0% superfat?
Which pot is safe for mixing lye solution?
quiz.explain: Stainless steel (or heavy HDPE/PP plastic) is safe. Aluminium, tin and zinc react with sodium hydroxide.

quiz.q: She has 200 g of caustic soda and wants a 33% lye concentration. How much water does she need?
quiz.explain: Water = 200 x 67 / 33 = 406 g (rounded).

modules.title: Laundry Soap Production at Small-Business Scale
modules.overview: Here you make a full 10 kg-oil production run of hot-process laundry bars, turn bars and offcuts into a soap-based laundry powder, and run the quality checks that decide whether a batch is ready to sell.

lessons.title: Hot-process laundry bars: a 10 kg production run
objectives: Prepare a batch sheet and equipment for a 10 kg-oil hot-process run
Bring the batch to trace and cook it through its stages
Test that the cook is finished before moulding
Mould, cut and dry bars so they are hard and ready for sale

blocks.text: In **cold process**, the soap is poured into the mould soon after it thickens and finishes reacting on its own over a day or two, then cures for weeks. In **hot process**, you keep heating the soap paste in the pot until the reaction is complete before it goes into the mould. For laundry bars, hot process suits a small business: the soap is fully reacted on the day, mistakes show up in the pot rather than weeks later, and bars only need a short drying period to harden.

blocks.name: cooking
blocks.alt: A pan cooking on a stove
blocks.caption: Hot process means cooking the soap paste gently until the reaction is complete.

blocks.text: Equipment for a 10 kg-oil run

items: Heavy-bottomed **stainless steel pot of at least 30 litres**. The batch weighs about 15 kg and swells while cooking.
Gas burner with a steady low flame, or a heat diffuser plate.
**Platform scale** for kilograms and a kitchen scale reading in 1 g steps for the caustic soda.
A long **stainless paddle**, and either a heavy-duty stick blender or a drill mixer with a stainless paddle. Hand stirring alone at this size can take a very long time to reach trace.
Thermometer, pH test strips, wooden or plastic block moulds lined with plastic sheet, a cutting wire or long knife, and drying racks.
All the protective equipment from Module 1.

blocks.title: Worked example: the batch sheet for a 10 kg-oil run
blocks.context: For example, Chinyere in Owerri makes laundry bars from 70% PKO and 30% palm oil at 2% superfat, with 98% caustic soda flakes and 33% lye concentration.
steps: Oils: PKO 7,000 g, palm oil 3,000 g; total 10,000 g.
Caustic soda at 0% superfat: 7,000 x 0.176 = 1,232 g; 3,000 x 0.142 = 426 g; total 1,658 g.
At 2% superfat: 1,658 x 0.98 = 1,625 g pure sodium hydroxide (rounded).
Corrected for 98% purity: 1,625 / 0.98 = 1,658 g of flakes to weigh.
Total wet batch: 10,000 + 1,658 + 3,299 = 14,957 g, about 15 kg.
blocks.result: Chinyere expects about 15 kg of fresh soap. After trimming about 300 g of edges, she can cut 73 bars of 200 g each. She checks the figures in SoapCalc before production day.

blocks.text: The production run, step by step

items: **Prepare.** Clear the area, put on protective equipment, and lay out every weighed material with its label. Tick each one on the batch sheet.
**Make the lye solution** outdoors: add 1,658 g of flakes slowly to 3,299 g of cold water in a stainless or HDPE container. Let it cool for about an hour.
**Melt the oils** in the big pot on low heat. PKO and palm oil are often semi-solid in cool weather. Turn off the heat once they are fully liquid.

**Combine.** Pour the lye solution slowly into the oils, down the paddle, with the flame off. Blend in short bursts and stir in between until the mixture thickens to **trace**: a drizzle leaves a trail on the surface.

**Cook.** Cover and heat on the lowest flame. Stir every 10 to 15 minutes. The paste thickens, may rise and foam (stir it down, do not let it overflow), then becomes smoother and partly translucent, a bit like petroleum jelly. A large batch often takes one to two hours; it is ready by test, not by the clock.
**Test** a small cooled sample (see below). If it fails, keep cooking and test again after 15 minutes.
**Mould.** Turn off the gas. Scoop the hot paste into lined moulds and press and bang the moulds firmly to push out air pockets. Smooth the top.

**Cut and dry.** The next day, unmould and cut bars with a wire or knife. Stamp your mark if you use one. Stand bars on racks with space between them, in a shaded, airy room, for one to two weeks before packing.

blocks.title: One hot-process production day
items: Weigh and mix lye
Melt oils, combine
Trace
Cook 1 to 2 hours
Test, then mould
Cut next day, dry
blocks.caption: Most of the day goes into the cook; the reaction is finished before the soap leaves the pot.

blocks.text: Is the cook finished?

Take a pea-sized lump, let it cool, rub it with a little water and test the lather with a **pH strip**. Well-made soap commonly reads about 9 to 10. A reading of 11 or more, or a lump that still looks oily or wet in the middle, means unreacted caustic soda or oil remains: keep cooking. Phenolphthalein drops turn pink in all soap, so they cannot tell finished soap from lye-heavy soap on their own.

blocks.title: Hot paste and fresh soap
blocks.text: Hot soap paste is as dangerous as hot oil and still caustic until the cook is complete. Wear gloves and goggles throughout, keep a long paddle, and keep children away from moulds. Treat any splash with running water straight away.

blocks.title: Why laundry bars still need drying
blocks.text: Hot process completes the reaction, but the bars still hold water. One to two weeks on racks makes them harder, so they last longer in a wet bucket and customers get more washes from each bar.

takeaways: Hot process finishes the reaction in the pot, so batch faults show on the day
Use a 30 litre or larger stainless pot for about 15 kg of soap
Cook on low heat, stir often, and judge by test not by time
pH about 9 to 10 is normal; 11 or more means keep cooking
Dry cut bars one to two weeks before packing

activity.title: Plan your production day
steps: Copy the 10 kg batch sheet and recalculate it for your own oils, superfat and caustic soda purity.
List your equipment and mark what you still need.
Write a timetable for the day, from setting up to washing tools.
Make a 1 kg trial with the same formula before your first full run.
activity.evidence: Your recalculated batch sheet, equipment list and a photo of your trial bars

lessons.title: Soap-based laundry powder from bars and offcuts
objectives: Explain how washing soda helps soap work in hard water
Grate, dry and blend laundry soap with washing soda safely
Run a simple wash test to set a dose
Calculate cost per wash for a powder batch

blocks.text: Many customers like powder for buckets and machines. Big factories make synthetic detergent powders by spray drying, which is beyond a small workshop. What you can make well is a **soap-based laundry powder**: your own dried laundry soap, grated fine, blended with **washing soda** (sodium carbonate, also called soda ash). It is also a good way to use offcuts and misshapen bars.

blocks.name: bucket
blocks.caption: A soap and washing soda powder is designed for bucket washing and top-loading machines.

blocks.text: What washing soda does

Washing soda is an alkaline salt. It softens hard water by tying up calcium and magnesium so they do not waste your soap as scum. It also helps lift greasy and sweat stains. It is not caustic soda and does not make soap by itself, but it is still an irritant: its dust stings eyes and the powder can dry and redden skin.

blocks.title: Handling washing soda
blocks.text: Wear gloves, goggles and a dust mask when pouring and blending. Blend with a lid on or in a closed container. Label the finished powder clearly, keep it away from children and food, and do not sell it in food or drink containers.
Making the powder

items: Use only fully dried hot-process laundry bars (at least one week on the rack). Wet soap clumps.
Grate the bars finely with a stainless grater or a dedicated grinder kept only for soap.
Spread the gratings on a clean tray in a shaded, airy room for a few days until they snap rather than bend.
Weigh grated soap and washing soda for your chosen ratio, for example 1 part soap to 1 part washing soda by weight for a first trial.
Blend in a closed container: shake or tumble until evenly mixed. Optional: a small amount of fragrance stirred in at the end.
Pack into sealed, labelled pouches or tubs at once, because powder absorbs moisture and cakes.

blocks.title: From bars to powder
items: Dried bars and offcuts
Grate fine
Air-dry gratings
Blend with washing soda
Pack and seal
blocks.caption: Every step depends on the soap being fully dry.

blocks.text: Setting a dose by testing, not guessing

Water hardness and how dirty the clothes are change the amount needed, so set your dose by a simple wash test. Use the same bucket, the same amount of water and similar dirty items for each trial, and record the result.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 5 kg powder batch and its cost per wash
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa in Jos has 2.5 kg of dried laundry bars and offcuts. Prices below are illustrative examples only; use your own receipts.
steps: She blends 2.5 kg of grated soap with 2.5 kg of washing soda: 5 kg of powder.
Wash test in a 10 litre bucket of warm water: 20 g leaves sweat marks on collars; 30 g cleans them; 40 g is no better. She sets her dose at 30 g per 10 litre bucket.
Doses per batch: 5,000 g / 30 g = 166 full doses.
Her costs for the batch: soap 2.5 kg at 1,400 naira per kg = 3,500 naira; washing soda 2.5 kg at 1,200 naira per kg = 3,000 naira; ten 500 g pouches and labels 1,500 naira. Total 8,000 naira.
Cost per pouch: 8,000 / 10 = 800 naira. Cost per wash: 8,000 / 166 = about 48 naira.
blocks.result: Hauwa can tell customers that one 500 g pouch gives about 16 bucket washes at her tested dose, and she knows each pouch costs her about 800 naira before her own time and profit.

blocks.text: Honest instructions for customers

items: Dissolve the dose in a little warm water first, so no soap flakes stay on dark clothes.
Not for wool or silk; washing soda is too alkaline for these fibres.
Rinse well. Soap can leave a dull film if clothes are not rinsed properly.
For front-loading machines that need low-foam detergent, advise customers to follow the machine maker's instructions; test before recommending your powder.

blocks.text: Getting the best from offcuts

Every production run leaves trimmed edges, bars that crack while cutting and bars with uneven stamps. These cost the same to make as perfect bars. Grating them into powder turns waste into a second product. Keep offcuts from each batch in a labelled, covered tray, and only use offcuts from batches that passed their pH and cut tests.

items: Store finished powder in a dry place, off the floor, with pouches sealed.
Write the batch code of the soap and the washing soda on each powder batch sheet.
If customers have very hard water, test a slightly higher share of washing soda, for example 1 part soap to 1.5 parts washing soda, and record the cleaning result.

blocks.title: What we leave out
blocks.text: Some home recipes add borax. It is not needed for a good powder, and this course leaves it out. Do not add bleach or acids to the powder.

takeaways: Soap-based powder = dried grated laundry soap + washing soda
Washing soda softens water and helps on grease, but irritates eyes and skin
Everything must be fully dry or the powder cakes
Set the dose with a recorded wash test
Know your cost per pouch and per wash

activity.title: Make and test a 500 g trial
steps: Grate and dry 250 g of your own laundry soap.
Blend it with 250 g of washing soda wearing gloves, goggles and a mask.
Run three bucket tests at different doses on similar dirty clothes.
Write your chosen dose and calculate cost per wash.
activity.evidence: A photo of your trial pouch with label, and your wash test notes

lessons.title: Quality control for laundry bars: tests, records and fixing faults
objectives: Run six simple acceptance tests on every laundry batch
Calculate drying weight loss as a percentage
Diagnose common laundry bar faults and their causes
Decide whether a batch is sold, reworked or discarded

blocks.text: Customers judge laundry soap on three things: does it clean, does it last in the bucket, and is it safe on hands. Quality control means checking these on every batch, writing the results down, and only selling what passes.

blocks.name: checklist
blocks.caption: A batch is ready for sale only when every test on the checklist has passed.

blocks.text: Six acceptance tests

head: Test
How to do it
Pass
rows: Cut one bar in half; look at the inside
Even colour, no oily pockets, no liquid, no white crystals
Wet lather on a pH strip
Press a thumbnail into a dried bar
Only a slight mark; bar does not bend
Weigh 5 marked bars at cutting and after drying
Weight has steadied (little change in the last few days)
Leave a bar in a wet dish for 2 hours
Only a thin soft layer, not a mushy bar
Wash a cloth with oil and sweat marks

blocks.title: Batch acceptance checklist
items: Cut surface even
pH about 9 to 10
Hard after drying
Weight has steadied
Passes wet dish test
Cleans test cloth
blocks.caption: Record each tick on the batch sheet with the date and your initials.

blocks.text: Tracking drying with weight loss

Weight loss shows how much water has left the bar. Weigh the same five marked bars on cutting day and every few days. When the weight stops falling much, the bar is as dry as your room will allow. Weight loss percentage = (starting weight minus current weight) / starting weight x 100.

blocks.title: Worked example: accepting a batch
blocks.context: For example, Chinyere checks her 73-bar run from Lesson 2.1 before packing. She labels it batch LB-07.
steps: Five marked bars weighed 1,000 g in total on cutting day (200 g average).
On day 10 they weigh 935 g; on day 14, 930 g. The change has slowed to 5 g in four days, so drying has steadied.
Weight loss: (1,000 minus 930) / 1,000 x 100 = 7%.
Average dried bar weight: 930 / 5 = 186 g. She will print "Net weight 180 g" so every bar meets or exceeds the label.
pH strip reads 10, the cut surface is even, the thumbnail test passes and the test cloth comes clean.
blocks.result: Batch LB-07 passes. Chinyere records the results, the net weight decision and the date, and moves the bars to packing.

blocks.text: Retained samples and records

Keep two bars from every batch, labelled with the batch code, in a closed box. These retained samples let you check a complaint months later: you can compare the customer's bar with your own, test the pH again, and see whether spots or smells developed in storage or only at the customer's home.

items: Batch code and date made.
Oils used, with supplier and the date each was bought.
Caustic soda purity and the weight actually used.
Cook time and the pH reading that ended the cook.
Acceptance test results, number of good bars and number rejected.
Name of whoever made and checked the batch.

blocks.text: A real-use trial

Laboratory-style tests are not the whole story. Before you launch a new laundry formula, give three bars to people who wash clothes by hand every week, such as a laundry worker or a family with several children. Ask them to note how many washes each bar lasts, how it lathers in their water and whether their hands feel dry. Compare the answers with a popular bar they already buy. This tells you how your bar performs where it will actually be used.
Common faults and what causes them

head: Fault
Likely cause
What to do
rows: Too much water, too little caustic soda, or too much soft oil
Check weighing and formula; dry longer; adjust next batch
Very low superfat with high PKO, or overcooked and dried out
Cut sooner while warm; add a little palm oil or 1 to 2% more superfat next time
Cook not finished, poor mixing or a weighing error
Do not sell; recheck the batch sheet; test pH
Do not sell. Recheck sums and purity correction
Harmless; trim or steam off for looks
Old oils or oils high in linoleic acid
Use fresh oils, store bars cool, check suppliers

blocks.title: Never sell a lye-heavy batch
blocks.text: A bar with too much caustic soda can burn hands that use it every day. If a batch fails the pH test or stings, set it aside, label it "NOT FOR SALE", and get advice before trying to rework it. Correcting a lye-heavy batch needs exact calculation; if you cannot do it with confidence, dispose of it safely rather than sell it.

takeaways: Test every batch: cut, pH, hardness, weight, wet dish, cleaning
Weight loss % = (start minus now) / start x 100
Set net weight on the label below your average dried weight
Lye-heavy or oily batches are never sold
Record results so faults can be traced

activity.title: Run the six tests
steps: Mark and weigh five bars from your trial batch on cutting day.
Weigh them again every three days and calculate weight loss.
Run the pH, thumbnail, wet dish and cleaning tests.
Record pass or fail for each test with the date.
activity.evidence: Your completed acceptance sheet for one batch

quiz.q: Why is hot process a good fit for a small laundry soap business?
options: The reaction is finished in the pot, so faults show on the day and bars need only short drying
It removes the need for protective equipment
quiz.explain: Hot process completes saponification during the cook. Bars still dry for one to two weeks but do not need a long cure.

quiz.q: During the cook, a cooled sample gives a pH strip reading of 12. What should she do?
options: Keep cooking and test again after about 15 minutes
Add water and sell it as liquid soap
quiz.explain: A reading of 11 or more suggests unreacted caustic soda. Keep cooking and retest; if it never comes down, the formula or weighing is wrong.

quiz.q: Five bars weighed 1,000 g at cutting and 920 g after drying. What is the weight loss?
A customer wants to wash a silk blouse with your soap and washing soda powder. What should you advise?
options: It is fine on any fabric
Do not use it on silk or wool, as washing soda is too alkaline
quiz.explain: Washing soda is too alkaline for protein fibres such as silk and wool.

quiz.q: White powder appears on the surface of some bars after a few days. What is it most likely to be?
options: Unreacted caustic soda that makes the bar unsafe
Soda ash, which is harmless and only cosmetic
quiz.explain: Soda ash forms when the soap surface reacts with air. It is harmless and can be trimmed or steamed off.

quiz.q: Her dried bars average 186 g. Which net weight is safest to print on the label?
quiz.explain: Print a net weight a little below the average dried weight so every bar meets or exceeds what the label promises.

quiz.q: A 5 kg batch of powder costs 8,000 naira and the tested dose is 40 g. What is the cost per wash?

modules.title: Bath Soap Production
modules.overview: Bath bars are judged by how they feel on skin, so this module is about balance: a quick melt-and-pour line for gifts and samples, a cold-process bath bar designed with SoapCalc's quality numbers at a 5% superfat, and safe, honest use of additives, colours and scents.

lessons.title: Melt-and-pour bath bars for gifts, samples and quick orders
objectives: Explain what melt-and-pour base is and when it makes business sense
Melt, scent and pour a base without overheating it
Prevent bubbles and glycerin sweat in humid weather
Cost a melt-and-pour bar from your own receipts

blocks.text: **Melt-and-pour** soap uses a ready-made soap base that a factory has already saponified. You melt it, add scent and colour, and pour it into moulds. There is no caustic soda to handle and bars can be used as soon as they set. The trade-off is cost: you pay for someone else's soap, so each bar costs more and you control fewer ingredients. Many small makers use melt-and-pour for event gifts, hotel samples, children's shapes and fast orders, and cold process for their main bath line.

blocks.name: gift-box
blocks.alt: A person holding a gift box
blocks.caption: Melt-and-pour is ideal for gift sets, souvenirs and quick custom orders.

blocks.text: Choosing a base

items: **Clear glycerin base:** transparent, good for embedding shapes and bright colours.
**White base:** opaque, pastel colours.
**Speciality bases** such as goat milk or shea: sold by suppliers with their own ingredient list.
Ask the supplier for the full ingredient list (INCI names) and the recommended melting and pouring temperature. You will need the ingredient list for your label.

blocks.text: Making a batch

items: Cut the base into small, even cubes so it melts evenly.

Melt gently in a double boiler (a bowl over a pot of hot water) or in a microwave in short bursts, stirring between bursts. **Never let it boil.** Overheated base turns thick, rubbery and yellowish and may smell burnt.
Take it off the heat. Stir in colour, then fragrance at the rate on the supplier's sheet. Stir slowly to avoid bubbles.
Pour into clean, dry moulds at the temperature the supplier recommends.
Spray the surface lightly with **isopropyl alcohol (rubbing alcohol, 99%)** to pop bubbles.
Leave to set for a few hours, unmould, and **wrap each bar in cling film or shrink film straight away**.

blocks.title: Melt-and-pour in five moves
items: Cube the base
Melt gently, never boil
Add colour and scent
Pour and spray alcohol
Unmould and wrap
blocks.caption: Wrapping straight after unmoulding stops glycerin sweat in humid air.

blocks.text: Layers and embeds

items: Pour the first layer and let it form a skin that holds when pressed lightly.
Spray the surface with alcohol, which helps the next layer stick.
Pour the second layer slightly cooler than the first, so it does not melt through.
For embeds, cut small cubes of a contrasting colour from an earlier bar, spray them with alcohol and place them in the mould before pouring clear base over them.

blocks.text: Because the base is already soap, the price per kilogram is higher than for oils and caustic soda. Melt-and-pour makes most sense for small, custom or gift orders where design and speed matter more than the lowest cost per bar. For your everyday bath line, a cold-process formula you calculate yourself is usually cheaper per bar and fully under your control.

Your label must list the base's full ingredient list as given by the supplier, followed by what you added, such as fragrance (Parfum) and colour. Keep the supplier's sheet with your batch records so you can show where each ingredient came from.
Glycerin sweat

Melt-and-pour bases contain extra glycerin, which pulls water from the air. In humid places such as Lagos, Port Harcourt or Calabar, unwrapped bars soon look wet and beaded, which customers often mistake for a fault. Wrap bars tightly as soon as they are unmoulded and store them in a closed container.

blocks.title: Alcohol and heat
blocks.text: Isopropyl alcohol is highly flammable. Never spray it near a gas flame or a hot stove ring, and keep the bottle closed and away from children. Melted base can burn skin: pour slowly and keep a bowl of cool water nearby for burns.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing 10 guest bars
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma in Enugu receives an order for 10 small guest bars for a wedding. Prices are illustrative examples; she uses her own receipts.
steps: She plans 10 bars of 100 g: 1,000 g of white base. Her base cost 7,500 naira per kg.
Fragrance: her supplier's sheet allows up to 3%; she uses 2% of 1,000 g = 20 g. Her 100 ml bottle (about 100 g) cost 6,000 naira, so 20 g costs 1,200 naira.
Colour and alcohol: about 300 naira.
Packaging: 10 cling-film wraps and printed paper bands, 1,000 naira.
blocks.result: Ifeoma knows each guest bar costs her 1,000 naira before her time and profit, so she can quote with confidence instead of guessing.

blocks.title: Do not re-melt endlessly
blocks.text: Every re-melt drives off water and can scorch the base. Melt only what you will pour in the next few minutes and keep the rest sealed.

takeaways: Melt-and-pour needs no caustic soda but costs more per bar
Melt gently, never boil
Follow the supplier's fragrance rate and pour temperature
Spray alcohol for bubbles, away from flames
Wrap bars immediately to stop glycerin sweat

activity.title: Make and cost five sample bars
steps: Buy a small amount of melt-and-pour base and note its price and ingredient list.
Make five bars following the steps in this lesson.
Wrap them straight away and leave one unwrapped for comparison overnight.
Work out the cost per bar from your receipts.

lessons.title: Designing a cold-process bath bar with a 5% superfat
objectives: Design a bath bar formula using SoapCalc quality numbers
Calculate caustic soda and water for a 2 kg batch at 5% superfat
Make, insulate and cut a cold-process bath batch
Cure bath bars correctly before sale

blocks.text: A bath bar has to do several jobs at once: clean without stripping skin, lather well, stay hard in the soap dish, and last. Instead of copying a recipe, you can design one using the **soap quality numbers** in SoapCalc. Enter your oils, and SoapCalc predicts hardness, cleansing, conditioning and lather.

blocks.name: lotion-bottle
blocks.caption: A bath bar is a skin product first, so mildness is designed in from the start.

blocks.text: Reading the quality numbers

head: SoapCalc number
What it tells you
Suggested range
rows: How hard and long-lasting the bar is
How strongly it strips oil; high can feel drying
How mild and moisturising it feels
Big, fluffy lather (lauric and ricinoleic acids)
Dense, stable lather (palmitic and stearic acids)

blocks.text: These ranges come from SoapCalc's own help text. A laundry bar of 70% PKO goes far above the cleansing range, which is exactly what you want for clothes. For a bath bar, keep cleansing inside the range. In practice that usually means keeping PKO or coconut oil to about a fifth of the oils, and letting palm oil, shea and olive carry the rest.

blocks.title: The design loop
items: Choose oil percentages
Check SoapCalc numbers
Adjust one oil
Make a small test
Use and record
blocks.caption: Change one oil at a time, so you know which change made the difference.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 2 kg bath batch
blocks.context: For example, Zainab in Abuja designs a bath bar of 40% palm oil, 25% olive oil, 20% PKO, 10% shea butter and 5% castor oil. SoapCalc shows its numbers inside the ranges. She makes 2,000 g of oils at 5% superfat with 99% caustic soda.
steps: Grams: palm 800 g, olive 500 g, PKO 400 g, shea 200 g, castor 100 g.
At 5% superfat: 289.9 x 0.95 = 275.4 g, rounded to 275 g pure.
Corrected for 99% purity: 275 / 0.99 = 278 g of flakes.
Batch weight: 2,000 + 278 + 558 = 2,836 g. Cut as 120 g bars after trimming, about 23 bars.
blocks.result: Zainab's sheet shows exactly what to weigh. At 2% superfat the same oils would need about 284 g of pure caustic soda, so her 5% choice leaves roughly 9 g less lye and a milder bar.

blocks.text: Making the batch

items: Mix the lye solution outdoors with full protective equipment and let it cool.
Melt the palm oil, PKO and shea, then add the olive and castor oil, which cools the mix.
When the oils and lye solution are both warm, not hot (many makers combine below about 45 degrees Celsius), pour the lye into the oils.
Stick blend in short bursts, stirring between, until light trace. Add fragrance now if using.
Pour into a lined mould, tap out air, cover, and wrap in an old towel for 24 hours so it can heat evenly (gel).
Unmould and cut after one to two days, wearing gloves: fresh soap is still caustic.

blocks.text: Problems you may meet

head: Problem
Likely cause
Prevention
rows: Batch thickens suddenly in the pot (seizing)
Some fragrance oils speed up trace
Test new fragrances in a small batch; add them at light trace and stir by hand
Overheating, often with honey or milk
Keep the mould cooler; do not insulate heat-raising batches
Oily layer on top after a day
Poor mixing or a weighing mistake
Blend to a true trace; check your weights
Cover the mould; harmless, can be planed off

blocks.text: Cut bars to the same size using a simple guide, such as a wooden box with a slot, so every bar has the same weight. A clean, even cut and a bevelled edge (shaved with a vegetable peeler after a few days) make a bath bar look professional. Use the shavings for samples or melt-and-pour embeds.
Curing

Cold-process bath bars must **cure for 4 to 6 weeks** on racks in a shaded, airy room. During this time saponification completes and water evaporates, giving a harder, milder and longer-lasting bar. Weigh marked bars as you did for laundry bars, and do a pH strip test before sale.

blocks.title: Hot process works for bath bars too
blocks.text: You can cook a bath formula by the hot-process method from Module 2. Add fragrance and any extra superfat oil after the cook, when the paste has cooled a little. The texture is more rustic, but the bars can be used sooner, though they still benefit from a couple of weeks of drying.

blocks.title: Fresh soap is caustic
blocks.text: Until it has cured, raw soap can irritate skin. Wear gloves to cut and handle it, and keep curing racks out of children's reach.

takeaways: Design with SoapCalc: hardness 29 to 54, cleansing 12 to 22, conditioning 44 to 69
Keep PKO or coconut to about a fifth of a bath formula
5% superfat is the standard bath choice
Combine oils and lye warm, not hot, and insulate for gel
Cure cold-process bath bars 4 to 6 weeks before sale

steps: Enter Zainab's formula in SoapCalc and note the five quality numbers.
Change one oil (for example swap 10% olive for groundnut oil) and note what moves.
Calculate caustic soda and water for a 500 g oil test of your chosen formula at 5% superfat.
Make the test batch and start a curing record.

lessons.title: Additives, colours and scents: safe amounts and honest claims
objectives: Choose skin-friendly additives and use them at sensible starting amounts
Use fragrance and essential oils within the supplier's limits
Refuse dangerous ingredients such as mercury and skin-bleaching agents
Describe your soap with cosmetic, not medical, claims

blocks.text: Additives make a bath bar distinctive: a clay bar for oily skin, an oatmeal bar for a gentle scrub, a honey bar for a warm colour. Used well they add value. Used carelessly they cause overheating, scratchy bars, skin irritation or dishonest promises.

blocks.name: honey-pot
blocks.caption: Natural additives like honey add appeal but need small, measured amounts.

blocks.text: Common additives and starting amounts

head: Additive
Starting amount
Notes
rows: Mix with a little of the batch water first to avoid lumps
Gives grey to black colour; too much leaves grey lather
Grind fine; coarse oats feel scratchy
Adds heat; dilute in warm water, keep the mould cool to avoid cracking
Gives yellow colour but can stain towels

blocks.text: These are starting points used by many hobby and small-scale makers. Test any new additive in a small batch, use it, and record the result before adding it to your range.
Fragrance and essential oils

items: Use only cosmetic-grade fragrance oils or essential oils from a supplier who gives a safety data sheet and a maximum use rate for soap. **Never exceed that rate.**
Some essential oils, such as cinnamon and clove, can irritate skin. Leave them out of a beginner's range.
Some fragrances turn soap brown over time (often those with vanilla notes). Test in a small bar and watch it for two weeks.
Never use perfume sprays, food flavourings or kerosene-based scents.

blocks.title: Decide additives in this order
items: Skin safety
Honest claims
How the bar performs
Colour and look
Scent
blocks.caption: Safety sits at the base: a beautiful scent never justifies an ingredient that harms skin.

blocks.title: Never add mercury or bleaching agents
blocks.text: The World Health Organization warns that skin-lightening products containing mercury are dangerous, and the Minamata Convention on Mercury restricts the manufacture, import and export of mercury-added cosmetics. Do not add mercury compounds, skin-bleaching chemicals, antibiotics or steroid creams to soap, and do not sell soap as a skin lightener.
Colour from local ingredients

You can colour bath bars without synthetic dyes. Red palm oil in the formula gives warm orange tones. Kaolin gives a soft cream. Activated charcoal gives grey to black. Turmeric gives yellow but may mark towels. Natural colours can fade in sunlight, so store bars away from windows and tell customers that colour may soften over time.
Testing a new additive

items: Make a 500 g oil test batch with only the new additive changed.
Write the additive, its supplier, amount and batch on the sheet.
Cure the bars fully, then check colour, scratchiness, lather and smell after two and four weeks.
Use the bar yourself and ask two willing adults to try it, recording what they notice.
Only add it to your range if it passes, and keep the amount the same every time.

blocks.text: Fragrance is calculated from the weight of oils, not the whole batch. For 1,000 g of oils at 2%, use 20 g; at 3%, 30 g. If the supplier's maximum is lower than the rate you planned, use the supplier's figure. Weigh fragrance on the 1 g scale and add it at light trace, stirring well.
Cosmetic claims, not medical claims

A soap cleans. You may say it "cleans gently", "has a light citrus scent" or "contains shea butter". You may not say it "cures eczema", "treats acne", "kills all germs" or "removes dark spots". Medical claims make your product a drug in the eyes of regulators such as NAFDAC, and they mislead customers. If a customer has a skin condition, advise them to see a health worker.

blocks.title: Worked example: adding clay and honey to a 2 kg batch
blocks.context: For example, Zainab turns her 2 kg bath formula from Lesson 3.2 into a clay and honey bar.
steps: Clay: 2,000 g of oils is 4 x 500 g, so 4 x 1 teaspoon = 4 teaspoons of kaolin. She mixes it with 4 tablespoons taken from her 558 g of batch water, so the total water does not change.
Honey: 4 x 1 teaspoon = 4 teaspoons, dissolved in 2 tablespoons of warm water, also taken from the batch water.
Fragrance: her supplier allows up to 3% of oils; she uses 2% of 2,000 g = 40 g.
Because honey adds heat, she does not wrap the mould in a towel and leaves it in a cool room.
Her label reads: "Clay and honey bath soap. Gentle cleansing with kaolin clay and honey." No medical claims.
blocks.result: The additives are measured, the water stays correct, the batch does not overheat, and the label promises only what a soap can deliver.

takeaways: Start small: about 1 teaspoon clay or honey per 500 g oils
Follow the supplier's maximum for fragrance and essential oils
Honey adds heat; keep the mould cool
Never use mercury, bleaching agents or medicines in soap
Make cosmetic claims only

activity.title: Plan one speciality bar
steps: Choose one additive from the table.
Calculate the amount for a 500 g oil test batch.
Write a label line that describes it without any medical claim.
Make the test, cure it and record colour, feel and any change after two weeks.

quiz.q: A customer complains that her melt-and-pour bars look wet and beaded after a week in Lagos. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The base was not cured long enough
Glycerin is pulling moisture from humid air; wrap bars tightly right after unmoulding
Too much caustic soda; discard them
quiz.explain: Melt-and-pour bases are rich in glycerin, which attracts water. Wrapping immediately prevents glycerin sweat.

quiz.q: SoapCalc shows a cleansing number of 30 for a bath bar formula. What should she change first?
options: Reduce the PKO or coconut oil and increase palm, shea or olive
quiz.explain: Cleansing comes mainly from lauric and myristic acids in PKO and coconut oil. Reducing them brings cleansing into the 12 to 22 range.

quiz.q: A bath formula needs 300 g of sodium hydroxide at 0% superfat. How much is needed at 5% superfat?
How long should cold-process bath bars cure before sale?
quiz.explain: Cold-process bars need 4 to 6 weeks for saponification to finish and water to evaporate, giving a harder, milder bar.

quiz.q: Which label statement is acceptable for a soap?
quiz.explain: Describe what the soap does cosmetically and what it contains. Medical and absolute germ claims are not acceptable.

quiz.q: How much kaolin clay should she start with for a 1,500 g oil batch, using 1 teaspoon per 500 g oils?
quiz.explain: 1,500 / 500 = 3, so 3 teaspoons.

quiz.q: Why should she not spray isopropyl alcohol on melt-and-pour soap beside a lit gas burner?
quiz.explain: Isopropyl alcohol is highly flammable. Keep it well away from flames and hot stoves.

modules.title: Packaging, Costing and Selling Your Soap
modules.overview: A good bar only becomes income when it is packed well, priced from real costs and sold to customers who come back. This module covers wrappers and labels for laundry and bath lines, a full costing of a production run, and the buyers and channels that keep a small soap business busy.

lessons.title: Wrapping, labelling and batch codes for laundry and bath lines
objectives: Choose packaging that suits laundry bars and bath bars
Write a complete, honest label with ingredients, net weight and warnings
Create a batch code system that traces every bar
Build a simple, consistent brand look

blocks.text: Laundry and bath soap are bought for different reasons, so they are packed differently. A laundry bar buyer wants value and a bar that does not melt in the bucket. A bath bar buyer is also buying a small pleasure or a gift. Packaging should protect the bar, tell the truth about it, and make your brand easy to recognise next time.

blocks.name: label
blocks.caption: The label is where your soap speaks for you when you are not there.

blocks.text: Packaging by product

head: Product
Common packaging
Why
rows: Printed paper wrapper or shrink film
Cheap, keeps bars clean, shows the brand
Easy to count, stack and resell
Paper box, kraft wrap or a paper belly band
Lets the bar breathe, looks handmade
Cling film or shrink film, then a band or box

blocks.text: What goes on the label

blocks.title: Label checklist
items: Product name and type
Ingredients, largest first
Net weight
Maker name and contact
Batch code and date
Directions and cautions
blocks.caption: Check every new label design against this list before printing.

items: **Ingredients**, from largest to smallest. Soap makers often use international (INCI) names for the soap made from each oil, for example Sodium Palm Kernelate (from PKO), Sodium Palmate (from palm oil), Sodium Shea Butterate, plus Aqua (water), Glycerin and Parfum (fragrance).
**Net weight** set below your tested average dried weight, as in Lesson 2.3.
**Your business name, address or phone number**, so customers can reach you.
**Batch code and date of manufacture.**
**Directions and cautions:** for example "For washing clothes. Keep out of reach of children. Avoid contact with eyes; if contact occurs, rinse well with water."
**NAFDAC registration number only once you have one.** Never print a number you have not been given.

blocks.text: A batch code that works

A batch code links every bar back to its batch sheet. Keep it short and logical, for example **LB-2610-07**: LB for laundry bar (BB for bath bar, LP for laundry powder), 2610 for year 2026 and month 10, and 07 for the seventh batch that month. If a customer complains, you can find the date, the oil supplier and the test results in minutes.

blocks.title: Worked example: two labels from one workshop
blocks.context: For example, Chinyere sells laundry bars and bath bars under her brand "Ada Clean" in Owerri.
steps: Laundry wrapper: "Ada Clean Laundry Bar. Ingredients: Sodium Palm Kernelate, Sodium Palmate, Aqua, Glycerin. Net weight 180 g. Batch LB-2610-07, made October 2026." Plus her phone number and the caution line.

Bath box: "Ada Clean Shea and Honey Bath Soap. Ingredients: Sodium Palmate, Sodium Olivate, Sodium Palm Kernelate, Sodium Shea Butterate, Sodium Castorate, Aqua, Glycerin, Kaolin, Honey, Parfum. Net weight 110 g. Batch BB-2610-02."
She uses the same logo, the same two colours and the same font on both, so customers recognise the brand on any product.
She prints labels on a single A4 sheet design at a local print shop and cuts them herself to keep the cost per label low.
blocks.result: Both products are honest, traceable and clearly from the same maker, which helps a customer who likes the laundry bar try the bath bar.

blocks.text: Brand basics

items: A short name that is easy to say and spell, and not already used by another soap brand near you.
Two or three fixed colours and one font. Use them on wrappers, WhatsApp posts and your price list.
Clear photos of your bars in daylight on a plain background for your catalogue.
One line that says what you stand for, for example "Hard bars that last the whole wash".

blocks.text: Storing finished stock

items: Keep wrapped bars in cartons in a cool, dry, shaded room, off the floor on pallets or shelves.
Stack cartons no more than a safe height and keep laundry and bath stock apart so scents do not transfer.
Sell oldest batches first and note on your stock sheet which batch codes are in each carton.
Keep soap stock away from caustic soda, fuel and food in a separate, labelled area.

blocks.text: Before printing a large run of wrappers, print ten, wrap real bars and leave them in your store for two weeks. Check that ink does not smudge, paper does not stain from the soap, and the label stays readable.

items: Wrap each bar in shrink film, leaving a little space at the ends.
Seal the ends with a heat sealer or warm the film evenly with a heat gun until it fits snugly.
Add the printed paper band or label so it covers the batch code area, or print the code directly on the band.

blocks.title: Pack only cured, tested soap
blocks.text: Never wrap bars before drying or curing is complete and the batch has passed its tests. Wrapped wet soap can sweat, soften or grow spots inside the wrapper.

takeaways: Laundry: value packs and cartons; bath: breathable, attractive packs
Labels need name, ingredients, net weight, maker, batch code, date and cautions
Print a NAFDAC number only after registration
A logical batch code traces every bar
Keep logo, colours and font the same across products

activity.title: Design your labels
steps: Write the full ingredient list for your laundry bar and your bath bar.

Draft both labels using the checklist in this lesson.
Show them to two people and ask what is unclear.

lessons.title: Costing a production run and setting wholesale and retail prices
objectives: List every cost in a production run, including labour and overheads
Calculate cost per bar from a real batch
Set wholesale and retail prices with a clear margin
Work out how many runs it takes to recover equipment costs

blocks.text: Many soap makers count only oil and caustic soda, then wonder why there is no money left. A correct cost includes everything the run uses: materials, gas, packaging, labour, and a fair share of rent and transport. This lesson costs Chinyere's 10 kg-oil laundry run from Lesson 2.1.

blocks.name: business-analytics
blocks.caption: A clear cost sheet shows exactly where each naira goes.

blocks.text: The cost sheet
The prices below are **illustrative examples only**. Raw material prices in Nigeria change often and differ by city, so replace every figure with your own receipts.

blocks.title: Worked example: from total cost to prices
blocks.context: For example, Chinyere's run gives 73 bars with a net weight of 180 g. She sells most bars wholesale to traders and some retail from her shop.
steps: Cost per bar: 42,540 / 73 = 583 naira (rounded).
Wholesale price: she sets 750 naira per bar. Profit per bar: 750 minus 583 = 167 naira.
Retail price: 900 naira per bar. Profit per bar: 900 minus 583 = 317 naira.
She expects to sell 48 bars wholesale and 25 retail: 48 x 750 = 36,000 naira; 25 x 900 = 22,500 naira; total sales 58,500 naira.
Profit for the run: 58,500 minus 42,540 = 15,960 naira, after paying her helpers and overheads.
blocks.result: Chinyere knows her floor price is 583 naira per bar. Any discount below that loses money, and every run that sells as planned earns about 16,000 naira on top of wages.

blocks.title: From costs to price
items: List every cost
Divide by good bars
Add your margin
Check market prices
Set wholesale and retail
blocks.caption: Price starts from your own cost, then is checked against the market, never the other way round.

blocks.text: Markup and margin are different

**Markup** is profit divided by cost. **Margin** is profit divided by price. At 750 naira wholesale, Chinyere's profit of 167 naira is a markup of 167 / 583 = 29% but a margin of 167 / 750 = 22%. At 900 naira retail, the markup is 54% and the margin 35%. Know which one a buyer or lender is asking about, because the numbers are different.

Use the same cost sheet for your other products. For laundry powder, the cost of the soap is your own cost per kilogram of bars, not the retail price. For bath bars, add fragrance, additives and the extra weeks of curing space, and remember a cold-process bath batch ties up money for 4 to 6 weeks before it can be sold.
When prices rise

Rerun the cost sheet whenever a main material changes price. If PKO rises from 2,600 to 3,000 naira per kg, Chinyere's 7 kg costs 2,800 naira more. Her run now costs 42,540 + 2,800 = 45,340 naira, and her cost per bar rises from 583 to 621 naira. Her wholesale profit per bar falls from 167 to 129 naira. She can absorb this for a short time, but if the higher price holds, she must adjust her prices or her formula, and tell her regular buyers early.
Recovering equipment costs

Equipment is bought once and used for many runs. Suppose Chinyere's 30 litre pot, mixer, moulds, scales and racks cost 150,000 naira (example figure). With a profit of 15,960 naira per run, she needs 150,000 / 15,960 = 9.4, so about **10 runs** to pay back the equipment. At one run a week, that is about ten weeks.
What changes the cost per bar

items: **Waste:** a failed batch still costs the full 42,540 naira. Quality control protects your profit.
**Bar size:** cutting 200 g wet bars instead of 220 g gives more bars per run, but the label must still be honest.
**Buying in bulk:** a 25 kg bag of caustic soda or a drum of PKO usually costs less per kilogram, but only if you can store it safely and use it before it spoils.
**Fragrance:** laundry bars sell well unscented; adding fragrance raises cost per bar.

blocks.title: Pay yourself
blocks.text: Include your own time as labour, even if you work alone. If the business only makes money when your time is free, it is not yet a business. Raise prices, cut waste or scale the run before you agree to sell below cost.

blocks.title: Keep the sheet on your phone
blocks.text: Set up the cost sheet once in Google Sheets or Excel with formulas. Each run, type in the new prices and bar count, and the cost per bar updates itself.

takeaways: Cost every run fully: materials, gas, packaging, labour, overheads
Cost per bar = total cost / number of good bars
Your cost per bar is your floor price
Payback runs = equipment cost / profit per run
Failed batches and waste raise the cost of every good bar

lessons.title: Selling to traders, laundries, hotels and gift buyers, and growing steadily
objectives: Identify buyers for laundry bars, powder and bath bars in your area
Set a wholesale price ladder that keeps your margin
Use WhatsApp Business and safe payment habits to take orders
Plan the next steps for growth, including registration

blocks.text: Laundry soap is an everyday product: customers buy again every week or month. Bath soap sells well as a treat and as gifts. A small business grows fastest by finding a few steady bulk buyers for laundry products, then adding bath soap for higher-margin orders.

blocks.name: business-shop
blocks.alt: A small shop front with a seller
blocks.caption: Steady wholesale buyers keep production running between bigger orders.

blocks.text: Who buys what

head: Buyer
What they want
How to reach them
rows: Cartons of laundry bars at a wholesale price
Visit with samples and a price list
Hard bars and powder in bulk, reliable supply
Laundry bars for students, regular deliveries
Speak to the bursar or matron
Show wrapped samples and your labels
Gift bars for weddings and parties

blocks.text: A wholesale price ladder
Bulk buyers expect a better price, but every step on the ladder must stay above your cost per bar. Write the ladder down and share it as a picture so it is the same for everyone.

blocks.title: Worked example: a price ladder that protects profit
blocks.context: For example, Chinyere's cost per laundry bar is 583 naira (from Lesson 4.2). A laundry business asks for a regular supply.
steps: Single bar, retail: 900 naira.
1 to 4 cartons of 12: 750 naira per bar, so 9,000 naira per carton.
5 cartons or more: 720 naira per bar, so 8,640 naira per carton. Profit per bar is still 720 minus 583 = 137 naira.
The laundry orders 5 cartons every two weeks: 60 bars x 720 = 43,200 naira per order.
Profit per order: 60 x 137 = 8,220 naira, with almost no selling effort after the first visit.
blocks.result: Chinyere gives a real bulk discount without ever going below her cost, and she plans production around this steady order.

blocks.title: The repeat-order cycle
items: Sample and price list
First order delivered
Check in after use
Reorder reminder
Bigger regular order
blocks.caption: Laundry soap is used up, so a satisfied buyer comes back if you keep in touch.

blocks.text: Taking orders on WhatsApp safely

items: Set up **WhatsApp Business** with your catalogue: photo, name, size and price for each product.
Post production days and new products on your status, with real photos of your own bars.

Take payment by bank transfer or through apps such as Moniepoint, Opay or Paystack links, and **confirm the money has arrived in your own account or app** before releasing goods. Do not trust screenshots of transfers alone.
Keep an order book: customer, product, quantity, price, date paid, date delivered.

blocks.text: Delivery and handling complaints

items: Agree delivery days with each bulk buyer and keep to them. Reliability wins more repeat orders than a small discount.
Carry stock in closed cartons so bars arrive clean and unbroken.
Count cartons with the buyer and give a simple receipt or invoice, even for cash sales.
Listen and write down the complaint, the product and the batch code on the wrapper.
Find the batch sheet and your retained samples, and test them.
If the fault is yours, replace the product or refund promptly and fix the cause.
If the soap passes every test, explain how to use and store it, for example letting bars drain between washes.
Record what happened and what you changed.

blocks.text: Handling complaints openly builds trust. A buyer who sees that you can trace a bar to its batch and test it again is more likely to give you a bigger regular order.
A weekly selling routine

items: Monday: check stock by batch code and update your WhatsApp catalogue.
Tuesday: message regular buyers whose last order is running low.
Wednesday: production or packing day.
Thursday: deliveries and collecting payments.
Friday: one new buyer visit with samples, and record sales in your order book.

blocks.text: Track which products sell fastest. If laundry bars sell out every week while bath bars sit on the shelf, put more of your production time into laundry runs and make bath soap mainly to order, for gifts and salons, so cash is not tied up in curing stock.
A fixed routine keeps sales steady even in weeks when production is busy, and it shows you which days and buyers bring most of your income.
Growing step by step

Grow in this order: first make every batch pass your tests, then find two or three steady bulk buyers, then increase run size or frequency. Before selling into supermarkets or across states, start the **NAFDAC registration** process for your products, and register your business name with the **Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)**. Many buyers ask for these before they will stock you.

blocks.title: Keep your records ready
blocks.text: Batch sheets, materials logs, test results and labels from this course are exactly the kind of records a regulator or a big buyer will want to see. Keep them together in one file.

takeaways: Laundry products bring repeat orders; bath bars bring higher margins and gifts
Every step on a price ladder stays above cost per bar
Confirm payments in your own account before releasing goods
Keep an order book and follow up for reorders
Register with CAC and start NAFDAC registration before selling to big retailers
